::: {.solutions}

Last session ended with a warning: from $A \Rightarrow B$ you may deduce one thing for free, and one
thing not at all. This session is about which is which.

There are **three** ways to rearrange an implication, and only **one** of them says the same thing as the
original. Getting them mixed up is the single most expensive mistake in Paper 2, because every
*"which of these is equivalent?"* question turns on it — and the exam writes them in English, not
symbols, precisely so that they are easy to confuse.

::: {.callout-important}
## Two words that are easy to swap — do not

It is the **contrapositive** that is always equivalent to the original. The **converse** almost never is.

A one-second check: **the contrapositive has negations in it; the converse does not.**
:::

Specification: **Arg1** — *the converse of a statement; the contrapositive of a statement; the
relationship between the truth of a statement and its converse and its contrapositive.*
Official source: **Notes on Logic and Proof**, pp. 43–49.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**What the codes mean.** Section 2 of the specification is numbered in three groups, and every session in
this toolkit is tagged with the ones it covers: **Arg1–4** (*arguments* — statements, connectives, *if*
and *only if*, converse and contrapositive, necessary and sufficient, quantifiers, negation),
**Prf1–5** (*proof* — direct, cases, contradiction, counterexample), and **Err1–2** (*errors* — finding
the flaw in a purported proof). They are a map, not something to memorise: when a Paper 2 question defeats
you, the code tells you which session to go back to.
:::

---

# Part 1 — Easy

Mechanical drills. Get the three rearrangements automatic before you try to judge them.

## Question 1

::: {.question}
Consider the statement

> **If $n$ is divisible by $6$, then $n$ is even.**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Write down its **converse**. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Write down its **contrapositive**. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Write down its **inverse** (negate both halves, keeping the arrow's direction). **[1]**

*Write your answers as full English sentences — the TMUA never asks for symbols such as $\lnot$ or
$\Rightarrow$, and every option on the real paper is written out in words.*
:::

Each of the three is made by one small operation, so [do them by the rule, not by the meaning]{.hl}:
the converse **reverses** the arrow, the inverse **negates** both halves, and the contrapositive does
**both**. Write $A$ = *"$n$ is divisible by $6$"* and $B$ = *"$n$ is even"* on your paper first — with
names in front of you it is almost impossible to go wrong.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — forming the converse, inverse and contrapositive
:::


Let $A$ = "$n$ is divisible by $6$" and $B$ = "$n$ is even". The original is $A \Rightarrow B$.

**(a) Converse** — reverse only, $B \Rightarrow A$:

> If $n$ is even, then $n$ is divisible by $6$.

**(b) Contrapositive** — negate **and** reverse, $\text{not }B \Rightarrow \text{not }A$:

> If $n$ is **not** even, then $n$ is **not** divisible by $6$.
>
> *(More naturally: if $n$ is odd, then $n$ is not divisible by $6$.)*

**(c) Inverse** — negate only, $\text{not }A \Rightarrow \text{not }B$:

> If $n$ is **not** divisible by $6$, then $n$ is **not** even.

$\blacksquare$

Now look at what you have. The original is **true**. So is the contrapositive (b) — as it must be. But
the converse (a) is **false** ($n=4$ is even and not divisible by $6$), and so is the inverse (c) — the
same $n=4$ breaks it.

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Giving the inverse when asked for the contrapositive | The contrapositive needs **both** operations. Negating alone is the *inverse*, and it is not equivalent. |
| "If $n$ is not even" left as-is when a cleaner form exists | Not wrong, but say **"if $n$ is odd"** — the exam's options are usually phrased naturally. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the three rearrangements

From $A \Rightarrow B$ there are exactly three things you can do:

| Name | Operation | Form | Equivalent to the original? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Converse** | reverse | $B \Rightarrow A$ | **No** |
| **Inverse** | negate | not $A \Rightarrow$ not $B$ | **No** |
| **Contrapositive** | **negate and reverse** | not $B \Rightarrow$ not $A$ | **Yes, always** |

**How to keep them straight.**

- The **contrapositive** is the only one with **two** operations — and it is the only one that is safe.
- The **converse and the inverse are contrapositives of each other**, so they are equivalent *to each
  other* — and both are unrelated to the original. (That is why they are true or false together: in
  Question 1, both (a) and (c) came out false.)

**A picture.** Read $A \Rightarrow B$ as "circle $A$ sits inside circle $B$".

- **Contrapositive:** *outside $B$ ⟹ outside $A$*. Look at the picture — if all of $A$ is inside $B$,
  then anything outside $B$ certainly missed $A$. **Same picture, read from outside in.** That is *why*
  it is always equivalent.
- **Converse:** *inside $B$ ⟹ inside $A$*. That would need the two circles to **coincide**, which is a
  genuinely different claim.
:::

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
ROOT_CLR, YINT_CLR, ASYM_CLR = '#1f77b4', '#2ca02c', '#d62728'

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 5.0))
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), 2.7, fc=YINT_CLR, alpha=0.10, ec=YINT_CLR, lw=2))
ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((-0.6, -0.2), 1.35, fc=ROOT_CLR, alpha=0.20, ec=ROOT_CLR, lw=2))
ax.text(-0.6, -0.25, '$A$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=15, color=ROOT_CLR)
ax.text(1.55, 1.75, '$B$', ha='center', va='center', fontsize=15, color=YINT_CLR)

ax.plot([3.7], [-1.9], 'o', color=ASYM_CLR, ms=10, zorder=5)
ax.annotate('outside $B$\n$\\Rightarrow$ certainly outside $A$\n(the CONTRAPOSITIVE — same picture)',
            (3.7, -1.9), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(-70, -52), fontsize=9, color=ASYM_CLR,
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color=ASYM_CLR, lw=1.2))

ax.plot([1.6], [-0.7], 'o', color='#7a5195', ms=10, zorder=5)
ax.annotate('inside $B$ but NOT in $A$\n$\\Rightarrow$ the CONVERSE fails here',
            (1.6, -0.7), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(26, 22), fontsize=9, color='#7a5195',
            arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='#7a5195', lw=1.2))

ax.set_xlim(-3.6, 6.2); ax.set_ylim(-4.4, 3.4)
ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
ax.set_title('“$A\\Rightarrow B$” = every $A$ is a $B$.\nThe contrapositive re-reads the same picture; the converse asks for a different one.',
             fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

## Question 2

::: {.question}
Assume this statement is **true**:

> *If it rains, then the ground gets wet.*

For each of the following, state whether it **must** be true, **must** be false, or **cannot be
determined**.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) If the ground is not wet, then it did not rain. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) If the ground is wet, then it rained. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) If it did not rain, then the ground is not wet. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(d) It rained and the ground is not wet. **[1]**
:::

Identify each one before you judge it: (a), (b), (c) are the contrapositive, the converse and the
inverse in some order. Only one of them is forced to be true. For (b) and (c), ask the honest question —
[could the ground be wet for some other reason?]{.hl} A burst pipe, a hose, a neighbour washing a car.
Part (d) is different in kind: it is not a rearrangement at all, but a claim that the original statement
is *broken*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — why the contrapositive is equivalent, and the converse is not
:::


Let $A$ = "it rains", $B$ = "the ground gets wet". Given: $A \Rightarrow B$ is true.

**(a) Must be true.** This is the **contrapositive** (not $B \Rightarrow$ not $A$). Dry ground rules out
rain, because rain would have guaranteed wet ground. ✓

**(b) Cannot be determined.** This is the **converse** ($B \Rightarrow A$). Wet ground is consistent with
a burst pipe. The original statement simply says nothing about it — [it might be true in some other
world, but it does not *follow*]{.hl}.

**(c) Cannot be determined.** This is the **inverse** (not $A \Rightarrow$ not $B$). Same reason: no rain
does not mean dry ground, because something else could wet it.

**(d) Must be false.** This says $A$ is true and $B$ is false — which is exactly the one combination
$A \Rightarrow B$ forbids. If it could happen, the original statement would be false.

$\blacksquare$

Notice that (b) and (c) received the same verdict. That is not a coincidence: **the converse and the
inverse are contrapositives of each other**, so they always stand or fall together.

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| (b) or (c) marked "must be false" | They are not *false* — they are **undetermined**. Nothing in the statement settles them either way. |
| (d) treated as a rearrangement | It is not an implication at all. It is the single case that would make the original **false**. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:7cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the one forbidden combination

$A \Rightarrow B$ makes exactly **one** promise: *you will never find $A$ true while $B$ is false.*
Everything else is permitted.

**How to read the table.** Each row is one possible situation — a combination of "is $A$ true?" and "is
$B$ true?". The last column asks: *would that situation make the promise a lie?*

| Row | $A$ | $B$ | Situation, in the rain example | Promise broken? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | true | true | it rained, ground wet | no — exactly as promised |
| 2 | true | **false** | it rained, ground **dry** | **YES** — the only way to break it |
| 3 | false | true | no rain, ground wet | no — a burst pipe; the promise said nothing about this |
| 4 | false | false | no rain, ground dry | no — again, nothing was promised |

**Rows 3 and 4 are why the converse and inverse cannot be deduced.** When $A$ is false, the statement
makes **no claim at all** about $B$ — so $B$ is free to be either. Row 3 is precisely the counterexample
that kills the converse.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Why this makes the contrapositive equivalent — slowly.**

Two statements are the same statement when they are **broken by exactly the same situations**. So ask,
for the contrapositive "not $B \Rightarrow$ not $A$", which row breaks *it*.

An implication is broken when its **front is true and its back is false**. For "not $B \Rightarrow$ not
$A$", that means:

- front true: &nbsp; "not $B$" is true &nbsp;$\longrightarrow$&nbsp; **$B$ is false**
- back false: &nbsp; "not $A$" is false &nbsp;$\longrightarrow$&nbsp; **$A$ is true**

So the contrapositive is broken when $A$ is true and $B$ is false — **row 2, the same single row** that
breaks the original. Same breaking condition, same statement. ∎

Now try the same test on the **converse** ($B \Rightarrow A$): it is broken when $B$ is true and $A$ is
false — that is **row 3**, a *different* row. Different breaking condition, different statement. That is
the whole distinction, in one calculation.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Proving something is false.** To show $A \Rightarrow B$ is *false*, you must produce a case where $A$
holds and $B$ fails — a **counterexample**. Part (d) is what a counterexample looks like: not "I disagree",
but a specific situation the statement forbids.
:::
:::

## Question 3

::: {.question}
Let $a$ and $b$ be integers. Consider

> **If $a$ and $b$ are both odd, then $ab$ is odd.**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Is the statement true? **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Write its converse, and decide whether the converse is true. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Write its contrapositive. Without doing any new work, say whether it is true and explain
how you know. **[2]**
:::

Part (c) is the point of the question, and it should cost you **no effort at all**: once you have settled
(a), the contrapositive's truth is [already decided, because a statement and its contrapositive are the
same statement]{.hl}. If you find yourself proving (c) from scratch, you have missed the shortcut this
whole session is about.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — judging a statement, its converse and its contrapositive
:::


**(a) True.** If $a = 2m+1$ and $b = 2n+1$ then

$$ab = (2m+1)(2n+1) = 4mn + 2m + 2n + 1 = 2(2mn + m + n) + 1 ,$$

which is odd. ✓

**(b) Converse:** *If $ab$ is odd, then $a$ and $b$ are both odd.*

This is also **true**. *(If either factor were even, say $a = 2k$, then $ab = 2kb$ would be even. So an
odd product forces both factors odd.)*

**(c) Contrapositive:** *If $ab$ is **not** odd, then $a$ and $b$ are **not** both odd* — more naturally,
*if $ab$ is even, then at least one of $a$, $b$ is even.*

It is **true**, and [we know this without any work: it is the contrapositive of a true statement, and a
statement and its contrapositive are always equivalent]{.hl}. Since (a) is true, so is (c). ✓

$\blacksquare$

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Watch the negation in (c).** The negation of "*$a$ and $b$ are **both** odd*" is **not** "*both are
even*" — it is "*at least one is even*". Negating an "and" flips it to an "or": that is Session 4, but the
trap is here already.
:::

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Proving (c) from scratch | Unnecessary. (a) true $\Rightarrow$ (c) true, automatically. That is the whole value of the contrapositive. |
| (c) written as "if $ab$ is even, then $a$ and $b$ are both even" | Over-negated. "not (both odd)" means **at least one** is even, not *both*. |
| Concluding from (b) that converses are usually true | Here both directions happen to hold — because "odd product" and "both factors odd" really are the *same condition*, so the pair forms an "if and only if". That is **unusual**: compare Question 1, where the converse was false. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:8cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — what you get for free, and what you must earn

| You have proved | You also get, free | You still owe |
|---|---|---|
| $A \Rightarrow B$ | its contrapositive, not $B \Rightarrow$ not $A$ | the converse $B \Rightarrow A$ |
| $A \Leftrightarrow B$ | everything — all four forms | nothing |

So when a question gives you a true statement and asks about a rearrangement:

1. Work out **which** rearrangement it is (converse / inverse / contrapositive).
2. If it is the **contrapositive** — done, it is true, no work needed.
3. If it is the **converse or inverse** — you must check it **separately**. It may be true, it may be
   false; the original tells you nothing.

**When the converse also turns out true**, as in part (b), the two statements are equivalent and you may
write them as one "if and only if". Many definitions are exactly this: *"$ab$ is odd **if and only if**
$a$ and $b$ are both odd."*
:::

# Part 2 — Medium

## Question 4

::: {.question}
Let $n$ be an integer. Prove that

> **if $n^2$ is even, then $n$ is even.**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Write down the contrapositive of the statement. **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Prove the contrapositive. **[3]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Explain why this proves the original statement. **[1]**
:::

Try proving the original directly and you will get stuck fast: "$n^2$ is even" gives you $n^2 = 2k$, and
extracting information about $n$ from that requires facts you have not been given. The contrapositive,
though, starts from "*$n$ is odd*" — and [an odd number has a formula you can actually compute
with]{.hl}, namely $n = 2m+1$. That asymmetry is the whole reason this technique exists.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — proof by contrapositive
:::


**(a) Contrapositive:** *If $n$ is **not** even, then $n^2$ is **not** even* — that is,

> **if $n$ is odd, then $n^2$ is odd.**

**(b) Proof.** Suppose $n$ is odd. Then $n = 2m+1$ for some integer $m$, so

$$n^2 = (2m+1)^2 = 4m^2 + 4m + 1 = 2\left(2m^2 + 2m\right) + 1 .$$

Since $2m^2 + 2m$ is an integer, $n^2$ is **odd**. $\blacksquare$

**(c)** A statement and its contrapositive are **logically equivalent** — they are true in exactly the
same circumstances. So having proved the contrapositive, [the original statement is proved as well; there
is nothing further to do]{.hl}.

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Proving the **converse** ("if $n$ is even then $n^2$ is even") instead | That is a different statement. True here, but it does **not** prove the original. |
| Writing $n = 2m+1$ and then forgetting to say *"for some integer $m$"* | The quantifier matters — it is what makes $2m^2+2m$ an integer at the end. |
| Stopping at $4m^2+4m+1$ | Not finished. You must display it in the form $2(\text{integer})+1$ to have shown it is odd. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — when to reach for the contrapositive

**The method.**

1. You want to prove $A \Rightarrow B$ and the direct route is awkward.
2. Write the contrapositive: **not $B \Rightarrow$ not $A$**.
3. Prove *that* instead.
4. Say the sentence: *"since a statement and its contrapositive are equivalent, the original follows."*

**The signal to use it.** Reach for the contrapositive when the **negations are easier to work with than
the originals**. Typical cases:

| Original hypothesis | Negation | Which is easier? |
|---|---|---|
| $n^2$ is even | $n$ is odd | the **negation** — it gives you $n = 2m+1$ |
| $x$ is irrational | $x$ is rational | the **negation** — it gives you $x = p/q$ |
| "at least one of …" | "none of …" | the **negation** — one case instead of many |

Anything of the form *"if [something about a square/product] then [something about the number itself]"*
is a strong candidate, because squaring is easy and un-squaring is not.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Not the same as proof by contradiction.** In a proof by contrapositive you assume **not $B$** and derive
**not $A$** — a clean, direct argument. In a proof by contradiction you assume **$A$ and not $B$** together
and derive an absurdity. They feel similar and are often confused; contradiction is Session 5.
:::
:::

## Question 5

::: {.question}
$P$ and $Q$ are statements. For each sentence below, write down its **contrapositive**, in the same
style of English as the original.

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $P$ only if $Q$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) $P$ if $Q$. **[2]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Hence explain why the contrapositive of *"$x>3$ only if $x^2>9$"* is *"$x^2 \le 9$ only if
$x \le 3$"*. **[2]**
:::

Do not try to negate an "only if" sentence directly — [convert it to "if … then …" first]{.hl}, take the
contrapositive there, and only then translate back if the question wants that style. Trying to shortcut
this is how people produce the inverse by accident. Recall from S1: *only if* keeps the order, a bare
*if* swaps it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — contrapositives of statements written with "only if"
:::


**(a)** "$P$ only if $Q$" means $P \Rightarrow Q$.

Its contrapositive is $\text{not } Q \Rightarrow \text{not } P$, i.e. *if not $Q$, then not $P$*. Written
back in "only if" style:

> **not $Q$ only if not $P$.**

*(Both are correct answers; the official Notes give exactly this pairing.)*

**(b)** "$P$ if $Q$" means $Q \Rightarrow P$ — the arrow starts at $Q$.

Its contrapositive is $\text{not } P \Rightarrow \text{not } Q$, i.e.

> **not $P$ if not $Q$** &nbsp; *(equivalently: if not $P$, then not $Q$).*

**(c)** Take $P$ = "$x>3$" and $Q$ = "$x^2>9$". The given sentence is "$P$ only if $Q$", so by part (a)
its contrapositive is "not $Q$ only if not $P$". Now negate each half:

- not $Q$ is "$x^2 \le 9$" &nbsp; *(the negation of $>$ is $\le$, not $<$)*
- not $P$ is "$x \le 3$"

giving exactly **"$x^2 \le 9$ only if $x \le 3$"**. ✓

$\blacksquare$

*Sanity check that it says something true: if $x^2 \le 9$ then $-3 \le x \le 3$, so certainly $x \le 3$. ✓*

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Negating $x > 3$ to $x < 3$ | The negation of "greater than" is **"less than or equal to"**: $x \le 3$. Forgetting the equality case is a standard TMUA trap. |
| Taking the contrapositive of (b) as "not $Q$ only if not $P$" | (b)'s arrow runs $Q \Rightarrow P$, so its contrapositive negates in the **other** order: not $P \Rightarrow$ not $Q$. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:8cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — the routine, and negating comparisons

**The routine for any awkward wording:**

$$\text{English sentence} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{“if … then …”} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{contrapositive} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{(translate back if asked)}$$

Never operate on the original English directly.

**The official Notes' table**, worth recognising:

| Statement | Contrapositive |
|---|---|
| if $A$ then $B$ | if not $B$ then not $A$ |
| $A$ only if $B$ | not $B$ only if not $A$ |

**Negating comparisons** — get these exactly right, because half-marks live here:

| Statement | Its negation |
|---|---|
| $x > 3$ | $x \le 3$ |
| $x \ge 3$ | $x < 3$ |
| $x = 3$ | $x \ne 3$ |
| $1 < x < 4$ | $x \le 1$ **or** $x \ge 4$ |

The pattern: **negating a strict inequality gives a non-strict one, and vice versa** — the boundary case
always changes sides.
:::

# Part 3 — Hard

## Question 6

::: {.question}
$m$ is a positive integer. Consider the theorem

$$\text{If } m^2 \text{ is divisible by } 4, \text{ then } m \text{ is even.} \tag{$*$}$$

Which of the following, **taken individually**, is/are equivalent to $(*)$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; If $m$ is odd, then $m^2$ is not divisible by $4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; If $m$ is even, then $m^2$ is divisible by $4$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; $m^2$ is divisible by $4$ only if $m$ is even.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** I only &nbsp;&nbsp; **B** II only &nbsp;&nbsp; **C** III only &nbsp;&nbsp;
**D** I and II &nbsp;&nbsp; **E** I and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **F** II and III &nbsp;&nbsp;
**G** I, II and III &nbsp;&nbsp; **H** None
:::

Name the halves and write $(*)$ as an arrow before you read the options — ten seconds spent there saves a
minute of confusion. Then classify each of I, II, III as *original / converse / inverse /
contrapositive*. Be warned that [all three statements happen to be **true**, so truth will not
discriminate between them]{.hl}; the question is which ones say *the same thing* as $(*)$.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — sorting several rephrasings at exam speed
:::


Let $P$ = "$m^2$ is divisible by $4$" and $Q$ = "$m$ is even". Then $(*) = P \Rightarrow Q$.

**I.** "If $m$ is odd, then $m^2$ is not divisible by $4$" is $\text{not } Q \Rightarrow \text{not } P$ —
negated **and** reversed. That is the **contrapositive**. **Equivalent.** ✓

**II.** "If $m$ is even, then $m^2$ is divisible by $4$" is $Q \Rightarrow P$ — reversed only. That is the
**converse**. **Not equivalent** — even though, as it happens, it is a true statement. ✗

**III.** "$P$ **only if** $Q$" is $P \Rightarrow Q$ — which is $(*)$ itself, word for word.
**Equivalent.** ✓

**Answer: E (I and III).** $\blacksquare$

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**Why II is the trap.** It is true, it is *about* the same two facts, and it feels like a restatement. But
$Q \Rightarrow P$ is the converse, and [a converse is a different claim even when it is a true one]{.hl}.
The question asks *"equivalent to"*, not *"also true"*.
:::

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| Including II because it is true | Truth is not equivalence. Compare the **arrows**, not the truth values. |
| Rejecting I because it "looks different" | It is negated and reversed — the definition of the contrapositive, always equivalent. |
| Missing III because "only if" was unfamiliar | "$P$ only if $Q$" is just $P \Rightarrow Q$ — the original, restyled. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — a 30-second exam routine

1. **Name the halves.** Write "$P$ = …, $Q$ = …" on your paper.
2. **Write the theorem as one arrow**, $P \Rightarrow Q$.
3. **Convert each option to an arrow**, using the S1 rules for *if* / *only if*.
4. **Match by shape**, not by meaning:

| What you see | It is | Equivalent? |
|---|---|---|
| $P \Rightarrow Q$ | the original (perhaps restyled) | ✓ |
| not $Q \Rightarrow$ not $P$ | contrapositive | ✓ |
| $Q \Rightarrow P$ | converse | ✗ |
| not $P \Rightarrow$ not $Q$ | inverse | ✗ |

**Never** let the truth of a statement enter this decision. Exam writers deliberately choose theorems
where the converse is *also* true (as here), precisely so that candidates who reason "it's true, so it
must be equivalent" get it wrong.
:::

---

## Question 7

::: {.question}
A student is asked to prove:

> **If $n^3$ is odd, then $n$ is odd.**

The student writes:

> *"Suppose $n$ is odd. Then $n = 2k+1$, so*
> $$n^3 = (2k+1)^3 = 8k^3 + 12k^2 + 6k + 1 = 2\left(4k^3 + 6k^2 + 3k\right) + 1 ,$$
> *which is odd. Hence if $n^3$ is odd, then $n$ is odd."*

&nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Is the student's algebra correct? **[1]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(b) Is the student's **proof** correct? Explain precisely what has been proved and what was
required. **[3]**

&nbsp;&nbsp;(c) Write a correct proof of the original statement. **[2]**
:::

Read the student's first line and the last line, and ask what was **assumed** versus what was **required**.
[The algebra can be flawless while the logic is wrong]{.hl} — that combination is exactly what Paper 2's
"find the error" questions are built from, and it is far harder to spot than an arithmetic slip.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

::: {.topic}
Topic — spotting a converse used as though it were a contrapositive
:::


**(a) Yes, the algebra is correct.** $(2k+1)^3 = 8k^3 + 12k^2 + 6k + 1$, and that equals
$2(4k^3+6k^2+3k) + 1$, which is odd. Nothing is wrong with any line of it.

**(b) No, the proof is not correct.** Look at what was assumed and what was concluded:

- The student **assumed** *$n$ is odd* and **derived** *$n^3$ is odd*. That proves
  $$(n \text{ odd}) \Rightarrow (n^3 \text{ odd}) .$$
- The question asked for
  $$(n^3 \text{ odd}) \Rightarrow (n \text{ odd}) .$$

So the student has proved the **converse** of what was required. [The converse is not equivalent to the
original, so nothing about the original has been established]{.hl} — the final sentence ("Hence …") does
not follow.

*It is worth noting that the statement the student proved is perfectly true, and so is the one they were
asked for. But proving one does not prove the other, and that is the error.*

**(c) A correct proof.** Use the **contrapositive**: *if $n$ is even, then $n^3$ is even.*

Suppose $n$ is even, so $n = 2k$ for some integer $k$. Then

$$n^3 = (2k)^3 = 8k^3 = 2\left(4k^3\right) ,$$

which is even. Since a statement and its contrapositive are equivalent, the original — *if $n^3$ is odd
then $n$ is odd* — is proved. $\blacksquare$

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The near-miss.** The student's work is only a small edit away from being right: had they *started* from
"$n$ is even" instead of "$n$ is odd", they would have had exactly the proof in (c). Choosing which
statement to assume is the entire skill here.
:::

**Common slips.**

| ✗ | ✓ |
|---|---|
| "The proof is fine because the algebra checks out" | Correct algebra proving the **wrong statement** is still a failed proof. Always compare *assumed* with *required*. |
| Fixing it by "reversing the steps" | The steps are not reversible as written. Restart from the contrapositive, as in (c). |
| Calling the student's error a contrapositive | They proved the **converse**. Their argument contains no negations at all — the giveaway. |
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:9cm"}
Working
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Concepts — auditing any proof in two lines

Whenever you are asked whether a proof is valid, ignore the algebra at first and write down two things:

$$\textbf{ASSUMED: } \underline{\qquad\qquad} \qquad\qquad \textbf{REQUIRED: } \underline{\qquad\qquad}$$

Then check the match:

| Assumed → concluded | Verdict |
|---|---|
| exactly what was required | ✓ valid (direct proof) |
| **not $B$** → **not $A$**, when $A \Rightarrow B$ was required | ✓ valid (proof by contrapositive) |
| $B$ → $A$, when $A \Rightarrow B$ was required | ✗ **proved the converse** |
| not $A$ → not $B$, when $A \Rightarrow B$ was required | ✗ **proved the inverse** |

**A quick tell:** a genuine proof by contrapositive **contains negations** — it starts from "suppose $n$
is *even*", "suppose $x$ is *rational*". If a student claims contrapositive but their argument has no
negation anywhere, they have almost certainly proved the converse instead.
:::

## Homework

**The main task — this is the one that covers today.**

1. **[Assignment: Converse and contrapositive](s02_assignment_student.qmd)** — 8 questions, **32 marks**,
   about 45 minutes.

**Then, to make it stick:**

2. **Notes on Logic and Proof, pp. 43–49** (*Converses and Contrapositives*). Note especially the
   discussion on p. 49 of *why* the converse/contrapositive mix-up happens.
3. **Ten statements of your own.** Write any ten "if … then …" statements about integers, and for each
   one write its converse and its contrapositive. Mark which are true. You should find the
   contrapositives always match the original, and the converses vary.
:::

**The whole session in one line:**

> **Reverse only = the converse, and it proves nothing. Negate *and* reverse = the contrapositive,
> and it is free.**

**Next session ([S3](s03_necessary_sufficient.qmd)): necessary and sufficient** — the same three arrows, dressed in the two words the
TMUA tests most often. You have already met them: *"$P$ is sufficient for $Q$"* is $P \Rightarrow Q$, and
*"$P$ is necessary for $Q$"* is $Q \Rightarrow P$ — so one of those two is secretly a converse.

:::
